x: Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours. 365.25 days is revolution and 29.78 km/s the orbital speed.
t: Discriminate rotation from revolution figures.

x: One revolution around the Sun takes about 365.25 days; 24 hours is one rotation.
t: Discriminate rotation from revolution figures.

x: The Coriolis effect deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.
t: Recall the deflection in each hemisphere.

x: Earth is at perihelion, nearest the Sun, around 4 January, and at aphelion around 4 July.
t: Discriminate perihelion from aphelion dates.

x: Option C is incorrect: Earth rotates west to east, counter-clockwise when seen from above the North Pole.
t: Check for a reversed direction.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the tilt changes the Sun's angle and day length as Earth revolves, which produces the seasons.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true, but the key treats R as a general trend: the effect is zero at the Equator because it depends on the sine of latitude.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the axis keeps its direction because of angular momentum; opposite seasons are a result, not the cause.
t: Check whether R is the cause or a result.

x: Rotation gives day and night, revolution the annual cycle, the centrifugal effect the equatorial bulge and the Coriolis effect deflection, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate effects of rotation and revolution.

x: At the summer solstice the Sun is over the Tropic of Cancer, at the winter solstice over Capricorn, and at both equinoxes over the Equator. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall where the Sun is overhead on each date.

x: Rotation is 15° per hour, one hour equals 15° of longitude, the axis tilts 23.5° from the perpendicular and orbital speed is 29.78 km/s, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the figures of Earth's motions.

x: I, II and IV are correct. III is false because local time advances eastward; moving west it falls behind.
t: Recall the direction in which time advances.

x: I, II and III are correct. IV is false because on 21 June the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day.
t: Recall day length on each date.

x: A is true: Earth moves fastest at perihelion. B is false because perihelion is in early January and aphelion in early July.
t: Check each statement for swapped dates.

x: The order is March Equinox, June Solstice, September Equinox, December Solstice, that is D, B, A, C.
t: Arrange the events by calendar month.

x: Three come from rotation: day and night, the Coriolis effect and time zones. Perihelion and aphelion belong to revolution.
t: Discriminate effects of rotation and revolution.

x: All three are correct: Earth's two motions are rotation, its spin on its axis, and revolution, its elliptical path around the Sun.
t: Recall the two motions of Earth.

x: The axis joins the poles, 1° of longitude equals 4 minutes, linear rotation speed is greatest at the Equator and zero at the poles, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the figures of rotation.

x: I, II and III are correct: the sunlit side has day, the far side night, and the circle of illumination divides them. IV and V are false because rotation, not revolution or tilt, causes day and night.
t: Discriminate effects of rotation and revolution.

x: Three are correct: 15° per hour, 1° in 4 minutes and 180° equal to 12 hours. Statement 4 is false because each time zone spans 15°, not 30°.
t: Check each figure with 360° in 24 hours.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the effect being strongest at the poles says nothing about its leftward direction in the south.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Rotation causes the centrifugal effect, which is greatest at the Equator, zero at the poles and causes polar flattening, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the features of the centrifugal effect.

x: Both are true: the axis joins the poles and makes 66.5° with the orbital plane, which is 23.5° from the perpendicular.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All three are correct: Earth moves on an elliptical orbit in about 365 days 6 hours 9 minutes, changing its position around the Sun.
t: Recall the facts of revolution.

x: Both are correct: at the summer solstice the Sun is over the Tropic of Cancer, giving northern summer, and at the winter solstice over the Tropic of Capricorn, giving northern winter.
t: Recall the solstice conditions.

x: All three are correct: equinoxes come twice a year with equal day and night; in March spring starts in the north, and in September autumn.
t: Recall the equinox conditions.

x: A is true: the Coriolis effect shapes cyclones. R is false because it comes from Earth's rotation, not revolution.
t: Check each statement for a swapped motion.

x: On 21 March and 23 September the Sun is over the Equator (northern spring and autumn), on 21 June over Cancer (summer) and on 22 December over Capricorn (winter), giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall where the Sun is overhead on each date.

x: At the September Equinox spring begins in the Southern Hemisphere and autumn in the Northern.
t: Recall the equinox seasons in each hemisphere.

x: Three are correct: on 21–22 December the north has its shortest day and longest night, and equinoxes bring equal day and night. Statement 4 is false.
t: Count the correct statements carefully.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the tilt keeps each pole facing toward or away from the Sun for half the orbit, giving six-month day and night.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: beyond the Arctic Circle daylight is continuous in northern summer, and beyond the Antarctic Circle in southern summer.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All four are correct: summer has direct rays and long days, and winter has slanting rays and short days.
t: Recall the contrast of summer and winter.

x: All four are correct: summer gets more solar energy and heating, and winter less.
t: Recall the contrast of summer and winter.

x: Aphelion is Earth's farthest point (about 152 million km) and perihelion its nearest (about 147 million km), giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Discriminate perihelion from aphelion.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Kepler's second law says equal areas are swept in equal times, so Earth moves faster near the Sun.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All five are correct: a normal year has 365 days, the extra quarter day adds up to one day in four years, and a leap year has 366 days with 29 February.
t: Recall the leap-year rule.

x: The Tropic of Cancer is 23.5°N, Capricorn 23.5°S, the Equator 0° and the Arctic Circle 66.5°N, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the latitude of each parallel.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the centrifugal effect, strongest at the Equator, causes the equatorial bulge and polar flattening.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Weight is least at the Equator and greatest at the poles, a longitude difference gives a local-time difference and the 180° meridian is the Date Line, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the effects of rotation.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: a tiny change in day length is a parallel effect, not the cause of the axis shift.
t: Check whether R is the cause or a parallel fact.

x: I, II and III are correct: melting ice moves mass toward lower latitudes and can shift rotation and the axis, and solar flares affect the upper atmosphere. IV is false because solar events were not the main explanation.
t: Discriminate the real cause from a distractor.

x: Rotation is Earth's spin on its axis. Movement around the Sun is revolution.
t: Discriminate rotation from revolution.

x: Earth revolves on an elliptical orbit, which is why it has a perihelion and an aphelion.
t: Recall the shape of Earth's orbit.

x: All seven are correct: rotation gives the centrifugal effect, time zones and Coriolis effect, while revolution with tilt gives seasons, solstices and equinoxes.
t: Discriminate effects of rotation and revolution.

x: Three come from rotation: time differences, the Coriolis effect and the centrifugal effect. Seasons come from revolution with tilt.
t: Discriminate effects of rotation and revolution.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the centrifugal effect is a separate result of rotation, not the cause of the Coriolis force.
t: Check whether R is the cause or a parallel fact.

x: Both are true: weight rises toward the poles and is greatest there.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Revolution is Earth's movement around the Sun. Spinning on its axis is rotation, and deflection is the Coriolis effect.
t: Discriminate rotation from revolution.

x: All three are needed: revolution, axial tilt and the axis staying parallel together produce the seasonal cycle.
t: Recall the causes of seasons.

x: At an equinox day and night are about equal everywhere, with the Sun overhead at the Equator.
t: Recall the equinox conditions.

x: In the Southern Hemisphere 21 March brings autumn, 21 June winter, 23 September spring and 22 December summer, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Reverse the northern seasons for the south.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the centrifugal effect is greatest at the Equator, so effective gravity and weight are least there.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Seasons come from Earth's revolution with its tilted axis. Distance from the Sun alone does not cause them; Earth is nearest in January.
t: Recall the causes of seasons.

x: Earth takes about 365.25 days to revolve around the Sun; 24 hours is one rotation.
t: Discriminate rotation from revolution figures.

x: On 21 June the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.
t: Recall where the Sun is overhead on each date.

x: At the Equator day and night are each about 12 hours all year. Six-month day and night happen at the poles.
t: Recall day length at the Equator.

x: Monsoon comes from the Arabic mausim, meaning season, because the winds reverse with the seasons.
t: Recall the origin of the word.

x: The keyed false statement is C, since seasons come from revolution with tilt, not rotation. Statement B is also inaccurate, because changing day length comes from revolution with tilt.
t: Discriminate effects of rotation and revolution.

x: Both are true and R explains A: direct rays and longer days give the summer hemisphere more heating.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: land and sea heat and cool differently, reversing pressure and therefore the monsoon winds.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: At the June solstice the Sun is over Cancer, at the December solstice over Capricorn and at both equinoxes over the Equator. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall where the Sun is overhead on each date.

x: On 21 March and 23 September the Sun is over the Equator, on 21 June over Cancer and on 21–22 December over Capricorn. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall where the Sun is overhead on each date.

x: Rabi is sown in October–November, kharif in June–July, zaid between rabi and kharif, and rabi is harvested in March–April, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall the season of each crop.

x: I and III are correct: around 21 June the north has its longest day and the Arctic has continuous daylight. II is false because the south then has its shortest day.
t: Recall day length on each date.

x: I, II and III are correct: monsoons reverse, blowing sea to land in summer and land to sea in winter. IV is false because land and sea breezes are daily.
t: Discriminate daily from seasonal winds.

x: Both are true: the Equator's day length hardly changes, and it has wet and dry seasons rather than winter and summer.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All four come from revolution with tilt: seasons, solstices and equinoxes, opposite seasons in the hemispheres and six-month polar day and night.
t: Recall the effects of revolution with tilt.

x: Both are true: the axis makes 66½° with the orbital plane, which is a 23½° tilt from the perpendicular.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: a changing position alone does not change the angle of the rays; the tilt is what does that.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: the axis stays parallel as Earth revolves, so each hemisphere in turn tilts toward and away from the Sun.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The angle of the Sun's rays and of insolation changes through the year. The rotation direction, orbital plane, tropics and axial tilt stay fixed.
t: Discriminate what varies from what is fixed.

x: The summer hemisphere tilts toward the Sun and the winter hemisphere away; summer has concentrated energy, a high Sun and long days, while winter has oblique rays and a low Sun, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the contrast of summer and winter.

x: All four are correct: day length, illumination and heating change through the year, and the changing heating gives seasons.
t: Recall the seasonal changes.

x: Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres, so summer in one means winter in the other.
t: Recall that hemispheres have opposite seasons.

x: At the June solstice the Southern Hemisphere has winter, the Northern its longest day, the North Pole tilts toward the Sun and the Equator has a 12-hour day, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the June solstice conditions.

x: Both are true: Arctic daylight can last six months, and the Equator keeps about a 12-hour day even at the June solstice.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: At the December solstice the north has its shortest day, the south its longest, the South Pole tilts toward the Sun and the Antarctic has continuous daylight, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the December solstice conditions.

x: All four are correct: solstices and equinoxes each come twice a year, with the Sun over a tropic at a solstice and over the Equator at an equinox.
t: Recall solstice and equinox conditions.

x: On 21 March the Sun is over the Equator moving north, on 21 June over Cancer turning south, on 23 September over the Equator moving south and on 21–22 December over Capricorn, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the Sun's apparent path through the year.

x: All four are correct: from September to December northern days shorten and southern days lengthen, and from December to March the reverse happens.
t: Recall day length on each date.

x: The north's shortest day and the south's longest are both 21 December, and the north's longest day falls in late June, usually 20 or 21 June. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-i, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall day length on each date.

x: Both are true: the North Pole has continuous daylight around June, and the South Pole around December.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true: the North Pole is dark around December, and the South Pole around June.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: R only defines the midnight sun; six-month day and night come from tilt and revolution.
t: Check whether R is the cause or only a definition.

x: All four are correct: the midnight sun occurs beyond the polar circles, peaks near each summer solstice, can give 24-hour daylight and is seen in Norway and other polar lands.
t: Recall the features of the midnight sun.

x: Both are true and R explains A: in summer the pole tilts toward the Sun, keeping it above the horizon all day.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: with the Sun over Cancer the north has summer and its longest day while the south has winter, and with the Sun over Capricorn the south has summer.
t: Recall the solstice conditions.

x: The tropics are 47° apart, each is 23½° from the Equator, and the December noon Sun at the Tropic of Cancer stands at 90° − 47° = 43°. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii.
t: Compute angles from 23½° on each side.

x: Both are true and R explains A: oblique rays spread the same energy over a larger area, so heating is lower.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: I and II are correct: the winter hemisphere gets more oblique rays and shorter days. III is false because direct rays fall on the summer hemisphere.
t: Recall the contrast of summer and winter.

x: A higher Sun gives a shorter shadow, a lower Sun a longer one, an overhead Sun none, and the Tropic of Cancer has almost no noon shadow on 21 June, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Relate Sun height to shadow length.

x: At the equinoxes the Sun is vertically overhead at the Equator, so there is no noon shadow.
t: Relate Sun height to shadow length.

x: Both are true: December is summer in the Southern Hemisphere, so Christmas in Australia comes in summer.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Perihelion is the minimum Earth–Sun distance, during northern winter, and aphelion the maximum, during northern summer, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate perihelion from aphelion.

x: Perihelion is about 4 January with faster speed, and aphelion about 4 July with slower speed, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Discriminate perihelion from aphelion.

x: Both are true: Earth is nearest the Sun in northern winter, so distance does not mainly cause seasons at either point.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds. Land, sea, mountain and valley breezes reverse daily.
t: Discriminate daily from seasonal winds.

x: The southwest monsoon runs June–September, the retreating monsoon October–November, the northeast monsoon matters for south-east India and traditional spring is March–April, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the timing of each Indian season.

x: All five are correct: the traditional seasons are summer in May–June, rains in July–August, autumn in September–October, pre-winter in November–December and winter in January–February.
t: Recall the traditional Indian seasons.

x: Both are true: kharif crops are harvested in October–November, and zaid crops grow in the short summer season.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All three are correct: mountain and valley breezes are periodic winds, summer heating makes low pressure and winter cooling makes high pressure.
t: Recall how heating changes pressure.

x: Both are true and R explains A: seasonal rainfall is what gives monsoon lands their wet and dry seasons.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Monsoons reverse winds seasonally, rabi, kharif and zaid are crop cycles, tropical deciduous forests show seasonal vegetation and insolation and day length set temperature, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall each seasonal effect.

x: All four are correct: the June solstice (20–21 June) is northern summer, and the December solstice (21–22 December) is northern winter and southern summer with the Sun over Capricorn.
t: Recall the solstice conditions.

x: A solstice has the greatest seasonal contrast and unequal day and night; an equinox is a transition with about equal day and night, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate solstice from equinox.

x: All five are correct: on 21–22 December the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn (23½°S), giving the north its shortest day.
t: Recall the December solstice conditions.

x: Both are true and the key takes R as explaining A: an axis at 66½° to the orbital plane is 23½° from the perpendicular, since the two angles add to 90°.
t: Relate the two angles that sum to 90°.

x: Both are true: rotation causes day and night, and winter has lower heating.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: At an equinox the Sun is over the Equator, on 21 June over the Tropic of Cancer, which lies at 23½°N, and the Tropic of Capricorn lies at 23½°S, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the latitude of each parallel.

x: Direct rays concentrate energy on a small area, giving greater heating. Spreading over a larger area is the effect of oblique rays.
t: Discriminate direct from oblique rays.

x: At the June solstice the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day and longest night.
t: Reverse the northern conditions for the south.
